newsitem.title: UK: World Bonds - EMU optimists should not omit Irish bonds.
newsitem.headline: World Bonds - EMU optimists should not omit Irish bonds.

text.p: Irish bonds will increasingly benefit as investors tire of Spain and Italy and look for alternative outlets for their enthusiasm over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said on Friday.

In the past month, Italian and Spanish bonds have rallied, narrowing the spread over German Bunds sharply on hopes that the Mediterranean countries will be part of EMU. But now those spreads have narrowed, investors are looking elsewhere.
"If you are going to be bullish, then why not buy a market with a good chance of being in the first round of EMU," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London.
"Ireland is going to meet the Maastricht criteria and should be trading like Belgium."

The spread of Belgian bond yields over Bunds was at 11 basis points, 0.11 percentage point, while that of Irish gilts was at 72 basis points. The benchmark 10-year Irish gilt was trading at 107.72, to yield 6.78 percent.

Ireland's budget deficit for 1997 was forecast at around 2.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), well within the 3.0 percent target set by the European Union's Maastricht treaty. Analysts said it was far more likely to be lining up at the start of EMU in 1999 than Spain and Italy.

Reed said Portugal, whose bonds have also been a beneficiary of EMU optimism, had an average inflation rate over the last five years of more than six percent, while Ireland averaged 2.4 percent over the same period.
Steve Englander, international economist at Smith Barney in Paris, said he felt the market was underplaying the risks of investing in the high-yielders and some people were starting to get jumpy.

"If you've made some money in the high yielders and you want a more conservative play, then try Ireland and Finland," he said. "It looks like rates are coming down over the next six months and at least you can go away for a weekend without worrying."
Englander said he expected the Irish gilt/Bund spread to squeeze to zero over the next year.
"The political will for EMU is apparent in Ireland and investors are starting to view Irish bonds less in tandem with U.K. gilts," he said.

Because of historic and economic links with Britain, analysts said Irish gilts were sometimes lumped in under the "anti-Europe' heading but analysts said those perceptions were increasingly misplaced.
However, Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London, said the lack of liquidity in Ireland's small debt market meant investors should be wary.
"It's like Switzerland. It's there but no one pays any attention to it," he said. "Small markets are easily squeezed."

On a spread comparison to British gilts, Shah said the Irish market was looking overstretched at a yield spread of 70 basis points. British 10-year gilts currently yield 70 basis points more than Irish gilts, compared with 20 in April.
"The spread has come in too far and will move back towards 50 points," he said.
He advised selling markets such as Finland and Ireland and buying British gilts, where the spread over Bunds would narrow to 135 points by the end of the year.
